item.title: Are You With Me or Against Me?
item.description:
Relationships

Are You With Me or Against Me?

Moving beyond “with me or against me” to foster deeper connection.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • When flooded, your prefrontal cortex goes offline and your relational thinking becomes binary: for/against me.
  • Black-and-white thinking blocks collaboration and often creates a victim triangle dynamic.
  • The way out is multiplicity, the ability to hold different parts of yourself at the same time.
Source: Assael Romanelli

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli.

Jamie and John keep yelling over each other in the session.

Finally, Jamie turns to me and demands: "Can you please tell John that what he's saying is not OK?!"

As a couples therapist, I've heard this a million times. I said, "Listen, Jamie, he has his own perception that's different than yours."

She looked at me. "So you're not going to back me up? Oh, I get it. I guess you're just like all the other therapists. Like all the other men. You take his side."

I actually wasn't taking anyone's side. I was doing my job: trying to hold two truths at the same time. But to Jamie, in that moment, there was no in between. Either I agreed with her completely or I was against her.

I meet this T-junction almost daily. Every couple I work with eventually gets stuck here. They stop being two subjects with two experiences and become two opposing sides fighting over one truth. With me or against me. Right or wrong. My truth or your truth.

That's not a character flaw. That's their flooded nervous system.

When you're flooded, when you're tense, tired, angry, or feeling unloved, your prefrontal cortex goes offline. The part of you that can hold complexity shuts down. What's left runs on one rule: threat or safe. With me or against me.

Such black or white thinking helped us survive. Thousands of years ago, if something approached you in the dark, you did not want to stop and consider its motives. You did not want to think, maybe it just wants to smell me. You needed a quick answer. Danger or not danger.

Where binary takes you

Every time I hear a client speak in such binaries, I know two things. They're flooded. And they're on the way toward the victim triangle dynamic.

The victim triangle has three roles or behaviors: victim, savior, and persecutor. People don't sit in one. They flow between all three, sometimes in a single conversation. Black-and-white thinking is what holds the triangle together, because the triangle runs on somebody being all wrong and somebody being all right.

A few nights ago I said something to my daughter and Galit corrected me right in front of her. I got so angry I stormed off. Standing in the bathroom trying to calm down, I kept ruminating. Galit is not OK. She's humiliating me in front of our kid. She's undermining my authority. I'm a good father. I don't deserve this.

article continues after advertisement

I felt that I was a hundred percent innocent and Galit was 100% guilty!

That's the triangle in one line. I'm the victim, she's the persecutor, and there's no third option available to me. After a couple of minutes of cleaving to my martyrhood, I started to realize what was happening. I wasn't thinking. I was flooded. I was in trauma mind.

We're not against all binaries. Sometimes they serve us well. But in a long-term committed relationship, binary thinking will hurt you. Not just your partner. Binary moves you away from collaboration and leads to an endless struggle over who's right. It leads to a one-narrative relationship: one of you as keeper of the "truth" while the other's truth is solely their "opinion." There is no synergy or synthesis, just reactivity and tiring conflict.

The opposite of binary

The way out is multiplicity. Multiplicity is the ability to hold different parts of myself at the same time, also called self-states. The angry part, the insulted part, as well as the part that knows I was out of line. Psychological maturity is the ability to access and shift between those self-states consciously.

Differentiation is the relational expression of that skill. It's my ability to hold on to myself and stay close to my partner. Not either/or. Yes, and.

Together they let you create a two-narrative relationship instead of a one-narrative fight, one in which both perspectives can co-exist and are equally valid. After all, subjective is the only objective in intimate relationships.

How to graduate from binary

Choose to believe that you're not a victim. If you want to step out of the binaries, you're going to have to believe this one, even if you fake it at first. And if you're not a victim, that means your partner isn't against you. They're just different from you, and that's what makes the relationship more interesting.

Notice. The next time you catch yourself in a with me/against me binary, in your head or out loud, understand that it's a signal. Not necessarily that your partner did something wrong. It's a sign that your nervous system is flooded and you're not seeing the full picture.

Breathe. Get your prefrontal cortex back online before you say anything else. Drink some water, shake your body, move.

article continues after advertisement

Use the "also" technique. Replace the words "always" and "never" with "also" and "sometimes." I'm also right. I'm also wrong. She also has a point. "Sometimes I feel like you're not listening to me," instead of "you never listen to me." These qualifiers don't weaken your truth. They make room for another truth next to yours. Your partner can be for themselves, and not against you.

"In my experience." Use this phrase as a way to own that it's just your experience, not necessarily the truth. The phrase also invites your partner to share their subjective experience. Two truths. Two narratives.

Play. Play is what will help you hold on to multiplicity. Play stops you from taking yourself so seriously. Play helps soften your exclamation points about your partner into question marks about your relationship. Have your curiosity outweigh your certainty. That's the first equation in the relational math of change.

Once you step away from binaries, from with/against me, you'll step into color, range, and newfound richness on the way to a richer, renewed marriage with your partner.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

item.title: 7 Signs You're Being Breadcrumbed
item.description:
Relationships

7 Signs You're Being Breadcrumbed

How someone keeps you emotionally invested without ever truly showing up.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • If someone only remembers you when you're finally moving on, you might be getting breadcrumbed.
  • Mixed singles are hard to walk away from and can leave you falling for someone's potential.
  • The moment you stop settling for breadcrumbs is when you make room for connection that actually nourishes you.
Source: Krakenimages/Shutterstock

Every time you finally convince yourself you're over them, your phone lights up.

"Hey stranger."

Suddenly you're smiling and making excuses for them. Maybe they've been busy. Maybe they finally realized what they want. Maybe this time will be different.

A few days later, it's back to radio silence.

If this cycle feels familiar, you may be experiencing breadcrumbing.

Breadcrumbing is a modern dating pattern in which someone gives you just enough attention to keep you emotionally invested, but never enough consistency to build a real relationship. Like the trail of breadcrumbs in Hansel and Gretel, each small interaction gives you hope that you're getting somewhere, only to leave you wandering in circles instead.

Here are seven signs you may be surviving on breadcrumbs.

1. They always come back... right when you're moving on

The minute you stop checking your phone every five minutes, come to terms with the fact that they're probably not interested, or finally agree to go on a date with someone else, they reappear. Sometimes it's a flirtatious text, sometimes it's an invitation you've been waiting for, and sometimes it's a crisis where you're suddenly the only one they can rely on.

It feels flattering and hopeful, but in reality, it's a strategic way to pull you back in just as you begin to emotionally detach.

2. They make plans like politicians make promises

They love talking about everything you'll do together one day, from the trip you'll take to the concerts you'll go to and the future you'll eventually share.

"We should totally plan a weekend away."

"I can't wait for you to meet my family someday."

The problem is that "someday" never becomes Saturday at 7.

Healthy relationships involve actual dates, actual times, and actual follow-through. Breadcrumbers often keep everything deliberately vague because possibilities don't require commitment. As long as the relationship remains hypothetical, they can enjoy the fantasy without having to take the risk of making it real.

3. They disappear without explanation and expect you to pretend nothing happened

One day you're texting regularly. Maybe you've even had a wonderful date or spent hours talking on the phone. Then, without warning, they disappear. Days pass, sometimes a week or even longer.

Just when you've accepted that they're gone, your phone lights up with a casual, "Hey, what's up?" or a reaction to your latest Instagram story.

You feel confused and taken aback by their nonchalance. Aren't they going to apologize or, at the very least, acknowledge that they vanished? But they're sweet, funny, and charming, and maybe this time things will be different.

Life gets busy, and everyone goes through stressful periods. Healthy relationships allow room for that. Emotionally mature people communicate when they need space, and if they intentionally or unintentionally disappear, they acknowledge the impact it may have had on the other person. Breadcrumbers, on the other hand, often expect you to hit the reset button every time they decide to come back.

4. They're watching your life without actually participating in it

They watch every Instagram story. They repost your funny cat videos. They like your vacation photos, but they still haven't responded to the text message you sent three days ago.

Breadcrumbing has become remarkably convenient in the age of smartphones. It takes less than a second to tap a heart or send a reaction. It takes considerably more effort to build a relationship.

Social media has made it easier than ever to create the illusion of closeness without becoming emotionally available. Someone can know what's happening in your digital world, react to every milestone, and still never truly show up in your real life (Balan, 2024)

They'll congratulate your promotion with a GIF of someone popping champagne, but never actually celebrate with you. Following someone's life online can create a false sense of intimacy, but real connection can't be built by showing up in someone's notifications.

5. You find yourself constantly decoding them

"Why did they text me at midnight?"

"What do two heart emojis mean?"

You find yourself replaying conversations, analyzing response times, creating intricate spreadsheets in your head, and looking for hidden meanings in every interaction.

Healthy relationships shouldn't require investigative skills. While every couple experiences misunderstandings from time to time, there should be room for honest conversations, even when they're uncomfortable. If you're spending more energy trying to interpret someone's behavior than actually experiencing the relationship, it's worth asking yourself why.

6. They seem incredibly interested... until you ask for something real

As long as the relationship stays undefined, they're fully engaged. They flirt, compliment you, talk about future adventures, and make you feel like something promising is just around the corner. They may even hint at introducing you to friends or family one day, making it seem as though the relationship is naturally moving forward.

The moment you want to have the talk and ask, "Where is this going?" things begin to shift.

Suddenly they're extremely busy or impossible to reach. Conversations that used to flow now feel like pulling teeth.

For many breadcrumbers, the fantasy is far more appealing than the reality. They can enjoy the excitement, validation, and companionship without the vulnerability or responsibility that comes with genuine commitment. But when the relationship requires honesty, accountability, or a decision, they often distance themselves.

7. You're in love with their potential

You find yourself making excuses for them. Maybe they're just scared. Once they find a job, things will settle down. When they're ready, they'll finally commit. Meanwhile, weeks turn into months, and sometimes even years.

Breadcrumbing is particularly difficult to walk away from because it operates through intermittent reinforcement. Occasional moments of warmth arrive unpredictably, which can make people even more emotionally invested because they keep hoping the next interaction will finally be different. It's the same principle that makes gambling so compelling. The occasional reward keeps people playing long after they should have walked away (Balan, 2023).

Healthy relationships, however, are built on concrete behavior, not endless potential. Someone doesn't prove they care through random bursts of affection. True connection requires showing up consistently, especially when it's inconvenient. That doesn't mean healthy couples never experience conflict or periods of distance. Ruptures happen in every relationship. The difference is that emotionally available partners take accountability, communicate honestly, and work toward repair instead of repeatedly disappearing and reappearing whenever it suits them (Johnson, 2019).

Breadcrumbing can leave people feeling anxious, confused, and questioning their own worth because it creates a painful cycle of hope followed by disappointment. Over time, some people begin lowering their expectations, convincing themselves that inconsistent attention is simply how modern dating works.

But whether it's modern dating or old-school romance, we all deserve genuine connection and respect. The truth is that you don't need occasional crumbs of affection to survive love. You deserve someone who doesn't leave you wondering where you stand because healthy love isn't built on mixed signals or empty promises. You deserve an invitation to the table.

item.title: Career Anxiety in the Age of AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Career Anxiety in the Age of AI

Parents can promote paths for success in the new AI career frontier.

Posted August 16, 2026

Key points
  • In 2026, new college graduates faced a tougher hiring market in areas affected by AI.
  • Parents of college students are increasingly concerned about the post-graduation job market.
  • Students can enhance their job prospects through internships, networking, and researching new opportunities.

"I’ve applied for 100 jobs and I’ve had a handful of interviews. Graduation is in two weeks and I’m worried I will be unemployed."

"My son just moved back home after graduation and does not have a job. Is AI making it impossible for him to get hired?"

Fears About Careers

As a psychiatrist, I have heard both college students and parents of undergraduates express concerns about the post-graduation job market. Fears have increased as AI and other factors impact the hiring landscape.

In a recent 2026 survey of 2,000 students, 69% worry about finding a job after graduation due to AI replacing certain human tasks. In a spring 2026 survey of 2,515 parents of college students, 29% report job prospects as one of their top five concerns, an 81% increase from 2024.

AI and Other Factors Are Slowing Hiring for New College Grads

Employer optimism about hiring new college graduates is at its lowest level in a decade, according to the College Hiring Outlook 2026. About 57% of employers believe hiring prospects are fair to poor for new college graduates in 2026, versus 18% of employers in 2024. At the same time, this report shows internships and co-op experiences can increase hiring, so seeking out these opportunities is critical for the post-college experience.

A survey of 2026 college graduates reflects findings similar to those of the business survey. Forty-three percent had a job offer by the time they graduated, a decrease from 2023. This study also demonstrates that doing internships, particularly paid ones, increases the chance of getting a job post-graduation.

While there could be several factors affecting the current employment trends for college graduates, many agree AI plays a role. A study from Stanford Digital Economy Lab demonstrates that early-entry employees aged 22-25 have experienced employment declines in certain fields such as software development and customer service. Jobs less affected by AI include those in healthcare, where AI can augment work without replacing it.

Whatever the impact of AI proves to be on the job market, it is critical that college students strategically pursue experiences that enhance their hirability.

Steps Students Can Take to Promote Job Success

Here are steps you can encourage your student to take to cope with career fears.

  1. Internships and co-op experiences. Most schools have career fairs where you can connect with recruiters about internships and jobs. You can also work with your professors to seek these opportunities. US News and World Report ranks schools with the best internship/co-op experiences.
  2. Career resource center. These campus centers can help you align your interests and talents with career options. Testing and coaching will help you gain a better understanding of what careers are a good fit.
  3. Find what you enjoy. You will spend many hours of your life at your job. Pursue a career that keeps you interested and makes you want to learn more.
  4. Network. If you are close to graduation and seeking a job, network with the people you know—friends and family—about opportunities. Don’t be shy about asking for help. Along the way, I've reached out to former college classmates and work colleagues who have helped me grow in my career.
  5. Take a college class in AI. Schools are offering more opportunities to gain deeper knowledge about the use of AI in the workplace. Learn about AI through a class or work experience—most jobs will want you to have AI knowledge and skills. In fact, in the 2026 survey mentioned above, 58% of college students said learning about AI is important for their career. Forty-eight percent think learning how to use AI ethically is a very important skill.
  6. Consider jobs in healthcare and teaching. In a June 2025 jobs report, healthcare and teaching showed growth in numbers of jobs, unlike other sectors of the economy. These areas seem resilient in the face of AI. As a psychiatrist, I don’t think my profession can be replaced by AI; a human connection and caring relationship improve patient outcomes. At the same time, AI has enhanced my ability to provide care by linking me with evidence-based treatment information in the OpenEvidence app. I look forward to seeing other ways AI can facilitate care.
article continues after advertisement

Our AI Journey: An Odyssey

If you are a parent of a college student worrying about AI impacting their career, remember that the unemployment rate in the second quarter of 2026 for new college grads (aged 22-27) was low at 5.7% and continues to be lower than that experienced by non-college graduates of the same age. There is no doubt that AI will impact job markets in profound ways, and it is critical that students connect with campus resources, network, and research the opportunities that exist for the future. View this career journey as an odyssey; your college student’s courage and curiosity will overcome challenges and lead to wonderful adventures.
